en: The Sūtra on the King of Cāṇḍālavaṭa Spoken by the Buddha, translated by the Song dynasty layman Juqu Jingsheng.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying in the kingdom of Śrāvastī at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, together with...
He was accompanied by twelve hundred and fifty bhikṣus.
At that time there was a king named Caṇḍa-vyaya, who served the path of the brahmins; whenever the king administered the affairs of state, he invariably employed various brahmins.
The junior consort, Lady Xiao, was treated with exceptional favor, and at that time she was also pregnant.
The other consorts, harboring hatred and jealousy toward her, gave gold to a Brahmin and instructed him to slander her to the King, saying:
"This woman is wicked; if she gives birth to a son, he will surely become a threat to the state."
When the king heard this, he became deeply distressed and unhappy, and asked the brāhmaṇa,
"What should be done? The brāhmaṇa replied:
"We should simply kill them both together.
The king said, "Human life is most precious; how can one kill it?"
He replied, "If you do not kill him, there will surely be the misfortune of the state's ruin and your own death; the calamity will not be small.
The king then followed his advice and had him executed, subsequently burying him.
Later, the child was born within the tomb; half of his mother’s body remained undecayed, and the child was able to drink her milk.
This continued for three years, until the tomb collapsed and subsided. The child subsequently emerged and played with birds and beasts, returning each evening to sleep within the tomb.

When the boy was six years old, the Buddha, out of universal compassion, took pity on him for his arduous toil as he lived among birds and beasts; he immediately transformed himself into a śramaṇa, went there dressed in monastic robes, and called out to him, asking:
"Whose son are you?"
"Where do you dwell?
The boy joyfully replied, "I have no home;
I merely reside in this tomb. Now, I beg to follow the practitioner."
The Buddha said, "I am going; will you follow me?
The boy replied:
"I shall now follow this man of the Way, whether my actions be good or evil.

The Buddha then led him into the Jeta Grove. Seeing the dignified deportment and the rules of discipline of the bhikṣus, he was deeply pleased in his heart and said to the Buddha, "I wish to request ordination as a bhikṣu."

The Buddha immediately granted his consent and stroked his head with his hand; his hair fell away, and the *kāṣāya* robe naturally clothed his body. He was named Sūda, and having received the noble precepts from the Buddha, he applied himself with diligent effort and an unwearied mind, attaining the path of an Arhat in seven days.
The Buddha said to Sudatta:
"Having received the noble precepts from the Buddha and uprooted the very foundation of desire, you have attained mastery over birth and death; you should now go to deliver that King Caṇḍapradyota."
Sudatta, receiving the Buddha’s instruction, prostrated himself with his head to the ground to pay homage to the Buddha.
He then went to that country and stood at the palace gate, requesting an audience with the king.
The ministers addressed the king, saying:
"There is a man of the Way outside who wishes to see Your Majesty.
Upon hearing this, the king immediately went out to meet him and asked:
"I have great cause for anxiety; what should I do about it?
The practitioner said, "What is it that you worry about?"
The king said, "I am already advanced in years and my time is passing; yet the kingdom has no heir to succeed me, for which I am filled with grief and anxiety.
When the practitioner heard the king's words, he initially did not respond, merely smiling to himself.
The king then spoke with indignation:
"I was conversing with this practitioner, yet he did not answer me at all, but instead laughed to himself.
He immediately intended to have him executed.

Śuddhoda understood his intention and immediately rose up, soaring through the air. He remained suspended in mid-air, dividing his body and dispersing his form, entering and emerging without interval.
When the king beheld these miraculous transformations of his majestic power, he was struck with terror and repented, saying:
"I am truly foolish and failed to distinguish the true from the false. I only pray that the Great Sage will return once more, so that I may take refuge in his life."
Sudatta immediately descended from mid-air and stood before the king, saying to him:
"If you can take refuge [in the Triple Gem], it is most excellent!
You should take refuge in the Buddha; the Buddha is my Great Teacher, the Honored One of the Three Realms, who delivers and liberates all sentient beings."
The king then commanded his ministers to prepare the carriage, intending to proceed to where the Buddha was.

By means of his supernatural power (*ṛddhibala*), Śuddhodana, in the time it takes to stretch out an arm, brought the king and the people together to the Buddha’s presence. They prostrated themselves with their heads touching the ground to pay homage to the Buddha, took refuge in the Triple Gem, and requested to receive the five precepts to become lay devotees (*upāsaka*).
The Buddha told the king:
"If you wish to know who this bhikṣu Sūta is, he is the son of a pregnant woman whom you previously had killed based on the slanderous words of a brahmin you employed."

After his mother died, the son was born within her tomb; there, he drank from the breast of his mother’s half-decayed body for as long as six years. Now, having followed me to practice the Way, he has reached this state.
Upon hearing the Buddha’s words, the king became even more terrified, unable to restrain himself.
The Buddha said:

“In the past, during the era of the Buddha Kauṣṭhila, there was a king named Bhoṣada. The king and three hundred million people within his realm all followed the king in making offerings to the Three Honored Ones.”

At that time, there was an ordinary man living in poverty and without a profession, who regularly worked as a hired herder for the wealthy families of the kingdom, tending several hundred head of cattle.
Seeing the king and the people making offerings to the community of bhikṣus, he immediately asked them, "What are you doing?"
The people replied, "We make offerings to the Triple Gem; we shall later obtain its blessings.
He then asked again:
"What kind of merit is obtained?
The people replied,
"If a person with a pure mind gives alms to the Three Honored Ones, they will dwell in peace, security, and nobility wherever they go, and shall suffer no hardship."
He then thought to himself:
"I live in poverty, merely working as a hired herdsman; I have no food or drink myself—how can I give alms?
He then thought again:
"You should simply go back and take cow's milk, boil it to make curd and butter, and offer it to the pure-minded bhikṣus.
The community of bhikṣus then offered this prayer of blessing:
"May you obtain blessings wherever you may be in every successive life; thereafter, as you pass through birth and death again and again, may you always receive such blessings."
"Sometimes he was reborn above as a deva, and sometimes below as a king or noble.
Later, when he was a king, he went out on a hunting excursion and saw a fine cow in the kingdom that was pregnant with a calf; the king then ordered men to seize and slaughter the cow.
The lady said to the king, "Do not let anyone kill her child.
Then the owner of the cow pursued and brought the calf back; he broke it away from the herd and took it to raise and protect it.
The master spoke in anger:
"I shall cause the king to become like this ox.
Thereafter, his spirit returned to become the king's son; before he was even born, his mother was killed by the king. If you wish to know who Sudāya was, it was precisely this person.
The woman who witnessed the wrongful execution was, at that time, the king’s consort;
the brahmin was Gopāla.

As for why Sudāyin was born from within a tomb, with half his mother’s body remaining incorrupt so that he might drink her milk and grow to maturity, it was because in a previous life he had offered curd and clarified butter to the community of bhikṣus.
The Buddha said:

"Sin and merit correspond to one another like a shadow following a form; there has never been one who performed good and did not receive blessings, nor one who committed evil and did not suffer calamity."
Upon hearing the Buddha’s discourse on the sutra, the king attained understanding and immediately realized the stage of *srotāpanna*.

The people of the kingdom all followed the king in revering the five precepts, practicing the ten wholesome deeds, and taking refuge in the Triple Gem; some among them attained the stages of *srotāpanna*, *sakṛdāgāmin*, *anāgāmin*, or *arhat*.
The fourfold assembly of disciples, as well as the devas, nāgas, and spirits, having heard the sutra, rejoiced; they came forward, paid homage to the Buddha, and departed.
This concludes the *Buddha-sūtra on King Caṇḍapradyota*.
